title: Caravaggio
intro: Michelangelo Merisi took his name from the town his family came from, east of Milan. In about fifteen years in Rome he changed how European painting handled light, and he did it while getting into court cases, sword fights and, in 1606, a killing.
He spent his last four years as a fugitive. His paintings are now spread across Europe, some still in the chapels they were made for.

chapters.place: Milan and the town of Caravaggio
chapters.heading: Training in Lombardy
chapters.text: Born in Milan in 1571 and raised partly in Caravaggio after plague killed his father. At 13 he was apprenticed to Simone Peterzano, a Milanese painter who said he had trained under Titian. Lombard painters liked plain, closely observed detail, and he took that with him. His Basket of Fruit, painted later in Rome, is in Milan's Biblioteca Ambrosiana.

chapters.place: San Luigi dei Francesi and Santa Maria del Popolo, Rome
chapters.heading: Fame in two chapels
chapters.text: He arrived in Rome broke and painted fruit and flowers for other artists. His break was the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi in 1600: the Calling of Saint Matthew, with a shaft of light across a tax office. Two more canvases for Santa Maria del Popolo followed. Both churches are free, and the paintings are still where he hung them.
chapters.image: Paintings by Caravaggio at Contarelli Chapel-3.jpg

chapters.heading: A death on the tennis court
chapters.text: In May 1606 a fight near the tennis courts on Via della Pallacorda ended with Caravaggio killing Ranuccio Tomassoni. He was sentenced to death in absentia, which meant anyone could kill him on sight, and he left Rome.
chapters.image: Caravaggio - David with the Head of Goliath - Vienna.jpg

chapters.heading: Sanctuary in Naples
chapters.text: Naples was Spanish-ruled and outside the Pope's reach. He was in demand at once: the Seven Works of Mercy, painted for a charity's chapel, still hangs over its altar. The Flagellation of Christ is at Capodimonte.

chapters.place: Valletta, Syracuse, Messina, Palermo and Porto Ercole
chapters.heading: On the run
chapters.text: In Malta he was made a Knight of the Order of St John, then jailed after another fight, escaped, and was expelled. He moved through Sicily painting altarpieces, went back to Naples, and was badly cut in the face outside a tavern. He died in July 1610 at Porto Ercole, on his way to Rome to ask for a pardon. He was 38.

chapters.heading: Where the paintings went
chapters.text: Collectors and dukes moved his easel paintings north. The Death of the Virgin was turned down by the church that ordered it and bought for the Duke of Mantua on Rubens's advice; it is now in the Louvre. The Taking of Christ was lost for two centuries and turned up in 1990 in a Jesuit house in Dublin.

title: Uprisings
intro: For forty-five years, people in Central and Eastern Europe kept trying to take their cities back. Most attempts were crushed within days or weeks. Each one was remembered, and in 1989 the anniversaries, the funerals and the songs came back.
Each stop is a place you can still stand in.

chapters.heading: Warsaw rises
chapters.text: On 1 August 1944 the Polish Home Army attacked the German occupiers, hoping to free the city before the Red Army arrived. The Soviets stopped on the far bank of the Vistula and waited. The fighting lasted 63 days. Up to 200,000 civilians died, and the Germans then destroyed most of what was left of the city.
chapters.image: Warsaw Uprising - Soldiers from Parasol on Warecka Street.jpg

chapters.heading: Builders strike in East Berlin
chapters.text: Construction workers on Stalinallee walked off the job over higher work quotas. Within a day hundreds of thousands were protesting across East Germany. Soviet tanks put it down, and dozens were killed.
chapters.image: Bundesarchiv B 145 Bild-F005191-0040, Berlin, Aufstand, sowjetischer Panzer.jpg

chapters.heading: Budapest fights the tanks
chapters.text: A student march on 23 October ended with Stalin's statue pulled down. Young fighters held the Corvin Passage against Soviet armour, and Prime Minister Imre Nagy announced that Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact. On 4 November the Soviet army came back in force. About 2,500 Hungarians were killed and 200,000 fled the country. Nagy was hanged in 1958.
chapters.image: 1956, Budapest, Üllői út - Ferenc körút, Kilián laktanya.jpg

chapters.heading: Students against the censors
chapters.text: When the authorities closed a production of Mickiewicz's play Dziady for being anti-Russian, students protested. The crackdown came with an antisemitic campaign that pushed about 13,000 Polish Jews to emigrate.

chapters.heading: The end of the Prague Spring
chapters.text: Alexander Dubček had promised “socialism with a human face”: less censorship, more debate. On the night of 20 August, Warsaw Pact armies invaded. In January 1969 the student Jan Palach set himself on fire at the top of Wenceslas Square in protest. Marta Kubišová's song “Modlitba pro Martu” became an anthem, and she was banned from performing for twenty years.
chapters.image: 10 Soviet Invasion of Czechoslovakia - Flickr - The Central Intelligence Agency.jpg

chapters.heading: A funeral, thirty-one years late
chapters.text: Hungary's government agreed to rebury Imre Nagy with honours. About a quarter of a million people filled Heroes' Square. It was the first sign that 1956 could be spoken about in public.

chapters.heading: The Wall opens
chapters.text: Erich Honecker had already been pushed out. At an evening press conference, a Politburo spokesman said the new travel rules applied “immediately”. Crowds went to the checkpoints, and at Bornholmer Straße the guards gave up and opened the gate.

chapters.heading: The Velvet Revolution
chapters.text: Police beat students on Národní street on 17 November. Within days, Wenceslas Square filled every evening. Václav Havel spoke from the Melantrich balcony, and Marta Kubišová, banned since 1970, stood up there beside him. By the end of December Havel was president.

chapters.heading: Ceaușescu's last speech
chapters.text: On 21 December Nicolae Ceaușescu addressed a rally from the Central Committee balcony, and the crowd booed him on live television. He fled by helicopter the next day. He and his wife were tried and shot on 25 December. Romania's was the only revolution of 1989 with heavy bloodshed: more than a thousand people died.
chapters.image: PSL during the Romanian Revolution of 1989.jpg

image: Berlin 1989, Fall der Mauer, Chute du mur 10.jpg

title: Songs of longing
intro: Many European cities have a song form built on missing something: a home, a lover, a country, a self. Most grew in port districts and poor quarters, often among people who had arrived from somewhere else, and most were looked down on before they became national treasures.
This one has no timeline. Start anywhere, and listen before you read.

chapters.heading: Saudade in the old quarters
chapters.text: Fado comes out of 19th-century Lisbon: sailors' bars, brothels and taverns in Alfama and Mouraria. The word for its mood is saudade, longing for something gone or never had. Amália Rodrigues took it to the world in the 1950s, and UNESCO listed it in 2011.
chapters.tip: Fado houses start late, often after 9 pm. When a fadista sings, the room goes quiet and stays that way.

chapters.heading: Deep song across the river
chapters.text: Triana, across the Guadalquivir from the cathedral, was home to Gitano families, potters and sailors. The oldest flamenco, cante jondo or “deep song”, is about grief, prison and hunger. Niña de los Peines recorded it in the 1910s, when most of it had never been written down.
chapters.tip: Tablaos are shows for visitors. Peñas, members' clubs that often let in guests, are where locals listen.

chapters.heading: Songs for the people who left
chapters.text: Millions of Neapolitans emigrated to the Americas, and many of the city's songs were written for them. “Santa Lucia luntana” is sung from a ship pulling out of the bay. “Munasterio 'e Santa Chiara”, from 1945, asks whether it's true that Naples has been destroyed, after Allied bombs burned the church.

chapters.heading: One song, played everywhere
chapters.text: Rezső Seress wrote “Szomorú vasárnap” in 1933 and played piano most nights at the Kispipa in the old Jewish quarter. Translated as “Gloomy Sunday”, it went around the world, and the press gave it a reputation as cursed. Billie Holiday's 1941 version is the best known in English.
chapters.image: Akácfa utca a Rákóczi út felől nézve. Fortepan 15309.jpg

chapters.heading: Refugees in the port
chapters.text: After 1922 more than a million Greeks were expelled from Asia Minor, and many ended up in shanty towns around Piraeus. They brought the music of Smyrna's cafés, and in the port's hash dens it became rebetiko: bouzouki songs about exile, prison, drugs and love. The Metaxas dictatorship censored it in the 1930s.

chapters.heading: The voice of the old taverns
chapters.text: Maria Tănase sang the songs of Romania's lăutari, the mostly Roma musicians who played in taverns and at weddings. She was a star from the late 1930s to her death in 1963, and many Romanians still know her songs by heart.

chapters.heading: Songs for the new arrivals
chapters.text: From the 1960s, millions moved from the Anatolian countryside to Istanbul and built houses on its edges overnight. Arabesk, with Turkish folk tunes, Egyptian strings and lyrics about fate and heartbreak, was their music. State radio kept it off the air for years. It sold on cassettes from the wholesale blocks at Unkapanı.

title: The coffeehouse
intro: Coffee reached Europe through Istanbul, and the coffeehouse came with it: a public room where anyone who paid for a cup could sit, read and argue. Writers worked in them, spies met in them, and several governments tried to shut them down.
Every stop here is somewhere you can go.

chapters.heading: Where it started
chapters.text: The first coffeehouses in Istanbul opened in the 1550s, near the spice markets. Sultans and clerics tried more than once to close them as places of gossip and sedition. In the 19th century, Levantine families built the European-style café life of Pera, now İstiklal Avenue.
chapters.tip: Turkish coffee is served with its grounds. Let them settle, and stop drinking before you reach them.

chapters.heading: Spies on Terazije
chapters.text: Hotel Moskva's café opened on Belgrade's main square in 1908. Through two world wars and the Cold War it was where diplomats, journalists and agents watched each other.
chapters.image: Hotel Moskva and the fountain in Belgrade.jpg

chapters.heading: Six hundred coffeehouses
chapters.text: By 1900 Budapest had about six hundred coffeehouses. Writers had regular tables, editors ran magazines from them, and some cafés stayed open all night. Gerbeaud, on Vörösmarty Square, is the confectioner of the era that survived.

chapters.heading: A seat for the afternoon
chapters.text: Vienna's first licensed coffeehouse opened in 1685, two years after the Ottoman siege. By 1900 the coffeehouse was the city's living room: Café Central had chess players, poets and, for a while, a Russian exile called Trotsky. UNESCO lists the culture as intangible heritage.
chapters.tip: One coffee buys a seat for as long as you like. It comes with a glass of water, and you can ask for the newspapers.

chapters.heading: Art Nouveau rooms
chapters.text: Prague's grand cafés were built in the 1900s, when the city was rich and building fast. Kafka and his friends met in the Louvre on Národní; Café Slavia faced the National Theatre and later became a meeting place for dissidents.
chapters.tip: The café inside the Municipal House keeps its original 1912 interior.

chapters.heading: The poets' table
chapters.text: Between the wars, Mała Ziemiańska on Mazowiecka Street was where Warsaw's poets held court, with the Skamander group upstairs. It was destroyed with the rest of the city centre in 1944 and never reopened.

chapters.place: Grand Café, Karl Johans gate, Oslo
chapters.heading: Ibsen's lunch
chapters.text: In his last years in Oslo, Henrik Ibsen walked to the Grand Café at the same time every day, and people came to watch him arrive. A mural inside shows him among the city's writers and artists.

chapters.heading: The existentialists' café
chapters.text: During and after the war, Sartre and Beauvoir wrote most days at the Café de Flore, partly because it was heated. Paris café life goes back to the Procope in 1686, but it was Saint-Germain that made the café a symbol of intellectual life.
chapters.tip: Coffee costs less standing at the counter than at a table, and more on the terrace.
chapters.image: Café de Flore, 172 boulevard Saint-Germain, Paris 6e.jpg

chapters.heading: Pessoa's table
chapters.text: A Brasileira opened in 1905 to sell Brazilian coffee. Fernando Pessoa drank there, and a bronze of him sits at a table outside. Martinho da Arcada, on the Praça do Comércio, has been open since 1782.
chapters.tip: In Lisbon an espresso is “uma bica”.

intro: In 1968 protest moved across Europe in months, not years. Students in Warsaw and Paris, workers in France, reformers in Prague and singers in Barcelona had different enemies, but they were watching each other.
The chapters follow the calendar.

chapters.heading: A banned play
chapters.text: The authorities closed a production of Mickiewicz's Dziady for being anti-Russian. Students protested, police beat them at the university gate, and the government answered with an antisemitic campaign that drove about 13,000 Polish Jews to emigrate.

chapters.heading: Easter riots
chapters.text: After the student leader Rudi Dutschke was shot in Berlin on 11 April, students blamed the Springer press and blockaded its offices across West Germany. In Munich two people died. Schwabing, the student district, had just been the setting of the year's comedy hit, Zur Sache, Schätzchen.

chapters.heading: Barricades in the Latin Quarter
chapters.text: Police cleared the occupied Sorbonne on 3 May. A week later students built barricades in the Latin Quarter, and by the end of the month around ten million workers were on strike. De Gaulle called an election and won it in June.
chapters.image: Prenez vos désirs pour des réalités - 1968.jpg

chapters.heading: Students against the “red bourgeoisie”
chapters.text: Belgrade students occupied their university for a week, protesting unemployment and the privileges of party officials. Tito went on television and said they were partly right, and the protest ended.

chapters.heading: The tanks arrive
chapters.text: Dubček's Prague Spring had lifted censorship since January. On the night of 20 August, Warsaw Pact armies invaded. Crowds argued with Soviet soldiers on Wenceslas Square, and Marta Kubišová's “Modlitba pro Martu” became the song of the occupation.

chapters.heading: The stake
chapters.text: Lluís Llach wrote “L'Estaca” in 1968, a song in Catalan about pulling down a rotten stake together, at a time when Franco's Spain restricted the language. It became an anthem far from Barcelona; in 1978 a Polish version, “Mury”, was taken up by Solidarity.

chapters.heading: Astral Weeks
chapters.text: Northern Ireland's civil rights marches began that autumn, and students at Queen's University founded People's Democracy. In November Van Morrison released Astral Weeks, an album about the Belfast streets he grew up on, months before the city turned violent.

title: Mozart
intro: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756 and spent much of his childhood on the road, shown off by his father to courts across Europe. As an adult he went where the opera commissions were, until he settled in Vienna in 1781 and tried to live without a court job.
This route follows him to the rooms where his music was first heard, most of which you can still sit in.

chapters.heading: Playing for the empress
chapters.text: At six, Mozart played for Empress Maria Theresa at Schönbrunn with his sister Nannerl. The family story is that he slipped on the polished floor, was helped up by the young Marie Antoinette, and announced he would marry her.

chapters.heading: Writing down a secret
chapters.text: Allegri's Miserere was sung only in the Sistine Chapel in Holy Week, and copying it was forbidden. The fourteen-year-old Mozart heard it once and wrote it out from memory that evening. The Pope made him a knight a few months later.
chapters.image: Pope Pius VII in the Sistine Chapel A29940.jpg

chapters.heading: His first big opera
chapters.text: Milan's court theatre, then inside the Palazzo Reale, commissioned an opera seria from a fourteen-year-old. Mitridate, re di Ponto ran for more than twenty nights. The theatre burned down in 1776, and La Scala was built to replace it.
chapters.image: Veduta di tre quarti del Palazzo Reale di Milano.jpg

chapters.heading: Idomeneo
chapters.text: Munich's elector commissioned Idomeneo, and it opened in the little rococo Cuvilliés Theatre in the Residenz. A few months later Mozart quarrelled with his employer, the Archbishop of Salzburg, and was shown out of his service with a kick from the archbishop's steward.

chapters.heading: Ten years in Vienna
chapters.text: In Vienna he lived on concerts, teaching and commissions, and moved house more than a dozen times. The Domgasse apartment, the grandest, is where he wrote The Marriage of Figaro. He died in December 1791 at Rauhensteingasse, two streets away, with the Requiem unfinished.
chapters.tip: The Mozarthaus museum keeps the Domgasse apartment's rooms. St Stephen's, where he married and where his funeral service was held, is around the corner.

chapters.heading: The city that loved him most
chapters.text: Figaro was a bigger hit in Prague than in Vienna, and Prague commissioned the next opera. Mozart conducted the premiere of Don Giovanni at the Estates Theatre on 29 October 1787. The theatre still stands and still plays Mozart.

chapters.heading: A city he never saw
chapters.text: Both Figaro and Don Giovanni are set in Seville, a city Mozart never went to. The Barber of Seville, the prequel to Figaro, was written later by Rossini, and Seville still points out balconies from both stories.
chapters.image: Jardines de la plaza de Santa Cruz.jpg

title: Art Nouveau
intro: Around 1900, architects and designers in a dozen cities turned against historical styles and tried something new: curving iron, plant forms, tiles, glass and furniture designed to match the building. It had a different name nearly everywhere it went: Art Nouveau, Modernisme, Secession, Jugendstil, Liberty.
It lasted about twenty years, until the First World War, and much of it is still standing.

chapters.heading: Where it began
chapters.text: Victor Horta's Hôtel Tassel, a townhouse for a professor, is usually called the first Art Nouveau building: iron columns that branch like stems, and lines painted on the walls that carry on the curves. Horta's own house and studio nearby is now his museum.

chapters.place: Glasgow School of Art and Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow
chapters.heading: Mackintosh's Glasgow
chapters.text: Charles Rennie Mackintosh designed the Glasgow School of Art and, with Margaret Macdonald, the Willow Tea Rooms for Kate Cranston, down to the chairs and cutlery. The art school burned in 2014 and again in 2018. The tea rooms have been restored and serve tea again.

chapters.heading: The Métro entrances
chapters.text: For the new Métro, Hector Guimard designed cast-iron entrances that look like plants growing out of the pavement. Parisians called the whole style “style Métro”. Porte Dauphine and Abbesses keep the rare versions with glass canopies.

chapters.heading: Modernisme
chapters.text: In Barcelona the style became Modernisme and a statement of Catalan identity. On one block of Passeig de Gràcia, rival architects built houses side by side, including Gaudí's Casa Batlló. Lluís Domènech i Montaner's Palau de la Música, all glass and mosaic, opened in 1908.

chapters.heading: Liberty
chapters.text: Italians called it stile Liberty, after the London shop that sold the new designs. Milan's wealthiest examples are around Porta Venezia, including Palazzo Castiglioni, whose stone nudes over the door upset the neighbours enough that they were moved.
chapters.image: 9028 - Milano, C.so Venezia - Giuseppe Sommaruga, Pal. Castiglioni (1904) - Foto Giovanni Dall'Orto 22-Apr-2007.jpg

chapters.heading: The Secession
chapters.text: In 1897 Gustav Klimt and other artists left Vienna's official academy and built their own exhibition hall, with a dome of gilded laurel leaves and the motto “To every age its art, to art its freedom”. Klimt's Beethoven Frieze is in its basement. The Kiss, from 1908, is at the Belvedere.

chapters.heading: Mucha comes home
chapters.text: Alphonse Mucha made his name in Paris with posters of Sarah Bernhardt. Back in Prague he decorated the Lord Mayor's Hall in the Municipal House, the city's showpiece concert hall and café, finished in 1912. Two years later the war ended the style almost everywhere.
chapters.image: Casa municipal, Praga, República Checa, 2022-07-02, DD 09.jpg

title: Football cities
intro: In most of Europe a football club is more than a team. It can stand for a religion in Glasgow, a nation in Barcelona, a country that no longer exists in Belgrade. Grounds are places of pilgrimage and, more than once, of disaster.
Each stop is a stadium, with the story of what it means to the city.

chapters.heading: The Old Firm
chapters.text: Celtic was founded in 1887 by an Irish Marist brother to raise money for the poor of Glasgow's East End, and became the club of the city's Irish Catholics. Rangers became the club of its Protestants. In 1967 Celtic were the first British side to win the European Cup. In 1971, 66 people died on a stairway at Ibrox after a New Year derby.

chapters.heading: The Kop
chapters.text: Bill Shankly arrived in 1959 and built Liverpool into a winning club. The Kop, the huge standing terrace, adopted “You'll Never Walk Alone” in 1963. In 1989, 97 Liverpool fans died in a crush at Hillsborough in Sheffield. It took 27 years and a second inquest to establish that they had been unlawfully killed.
chapters.image: The Kop at Anfield Stadium, Liverpool - geograph.org.uk - 5885064.jpg

chapters.heading: After Munich
chapters.text: In February 1958 the plane carrying Manchester United home from a European tie crashed on take-off after refuelling in Munich. Twenty-three people died, eight of them players. Matt Busby rebuilt the team, which won the European Cup ten years later.

chapters.heading: More than a club
chapters.text: Under Franco, when Catalan was restricted, Barça's ground was one of the few places tens of thousands of people could speak and shout it together. “Més que un club”, more than a club, is painted in the seats. The stadium is being rebuilt while the team plays on.

chapters.heading: The other side of El Clásico
chapters.text: Real Madrid won the first five European Cups and became, for many Catalans, the club of the regime. The Bernabéu, in the middle of the city, has just been rebuilt with a steel skin and a roof that closes.

chapters.heading: A city's one club
chapters.text: Marseille has one big club, and the whole city follows it. In 1993 Olympique de Marseille became the first French side to win the Champions League. Its ultras groups run the two curves of the Vélodrome.

chapters.heading: Two clubs, one stadium
chapters.text: Inter was founded in 1908 by members who left AC Milan because they wanted to sign foreign players. The two clubs have shared San Siro since 1947. Under Helenio Herrera in the 1960s, Inter won two European Cups with a defensive style the world learned to call catenaccio.

chapters.place: FC Bayern Museum, Allianz Arena, Munich
chapters.heading: The Jewish president
chapters.text: Kurt Landauer was Bayern's president when it won its first German title in 1932. The Nazis forced him out the next year, and he survived the war in exile in Switzerland. He came back and was president again after the war. The club now honours him openly.

chapters.place: Red Star and Partizan stadiums, Belgrade
chapters.heading: The Eternal Derby
chapters.text: Red Star and Partizan were both founded in 1945, and their grounds are a short walk apart. In May 1991 Red Star won the European Cup in Bari, on penalties, with players from across Yugoslavia. Within weeks the country began to break up, and the team with it.

title: Jewish quarters
intro: Jews have lived in European cities for more than two thousand years. In many of them, the Jewish quarter was where they were allowed or required to live, and its streets, synagogues and cemeteries are among the oldest parts of town.
This thread goes roughly in the order the communities were founded. It includes the Holocaust, but it starts long before it, and in some cities it does not end with it.

chapters.heading: The oldest community
chapters.text: Rome's Jewish community is the oldest in Europe. The Arch of Titus shows Roman soldiers carrying the menorah looted from Jerusalem in 70 AD. In 1555 a pope walled Rome's Jews into a ghetto by the Tiber, which lasted until 1870. On 16 October 1943, the Germans rounded up more than a thousand people there; sixteen came back.
chapters.tip: Restaurants along Via del Portico d'Ottavia serve carciofi alla giudia, whole artichokes fried twice.

chapters.heading: Sepharad
chapters.text: Santa Cruz, now the most photographed quarter of Seville, was its judería. In 1391 riots against the Jews started here and spread across Spain. In 1492 the Jews who had not converted were expelled from the country.

chapters.heading: The first ghetto
chapters.text: In 1516 Venice ordered its Jews to live on a small island by an old foundry, a getto, which was locked at night. The word spread to the rest of Europe. With no room to expand, the buildings grew up to seven storeys, taller than anywhere else in the city.

chapters.heading: A refuge
chapters.text: Jews who had been forced to convert in Spain and Portugal found in Amsterdam a city where they could practise openly. Their Portuguese Synagogue opened in 1675 and is still lit by candles. In 1656 the community expelled one of its own, the philosopher Baruch Spinoza.

chapters.heading: The Old-New Synagogue
chapters.text: The Old-New Synagogue, from around 1270, is the oldest working synagogue in Europe. Legend says the clay Golem of Rabbi Loew lies in its attic. Next door, the Old Jewish Cemetery has graves up to twelve layers deep. Franz Kafka was born at the edge of the quarter.
chapters.image: Old New Synagogue- Jewish Town Hall (Prague).jpg

chapters.heading: Kazimierz
chapters.text: King Casimir founded Kazimierz as a separate town in 1335, and from 1495 Kraków's Jews lived there. In 1941 the Germans moved them across the river into a ghetto in Podgórze. Since the 1990s Kazimierz has come back to life, with restored synagogues and an annual Jewish Culture Festival.
chapters.image: Wolf Popper Synagogue, Entrance gate, 16 Szeroka street, Kazimierz, Kraków, Poland.jpg

chapters.heading: The largest community in Europe
chapters.text: Before the war, about a third of Warsaw was Jewish. Isaac Bashevis Singer grew up on Krochmalna Street, and Janusz Korczak ran his orphanage nearby. In 1940 the Germans sealed off the ghetto. In April 1943 its last inhabitants rose up, and the Germans burned it street by street.

chapters.heading: Europe's largest synagogue
chapters.text: The Dohány Street Synagogue, finished in 1859, seats about three thousand. Theodor Herzl, who imagined a Jewish state, was born next door. In 1944 Hungary's Jews were deported in a few weeks; in Budapest, Raoul Wallenberg and other diplomats saved thousands with protective passes.

chapters.heading: A family's netsuke
chapters.text: Vienna around 1900 was shaped by Jewish families: bankers, doctors, writers, composers. Edmund de Waal traced one of them, the Ephrussis, through a collection of Japanese netsuke hidden by a maid during the war. The Holocaust memorial on Judenplatz is a library whose books cannot be opened.

chapters.heading: Across the Sound
chapters.text: When word came in 1943 that Denmark's Jews were to be deported, ordinary Danes hid them and ferried about 7,000 across the water to neutral Sweden in a few weeks. Most of the community survived.

image: Old Jewish Cemetery in Josefov, Prague - 8363.jpg

title: The Atlantic slave trade
intro: For four centuries, European ships carried about 12.5 million Africans across the Atlantic to forced labour in the Americas. The trade was run from Europe's ports, and the money built warehouses, banks, town halls and country houses that are still there.
Each city here has started, at different speeds, to say so in public.

chapters.heading: Where it started
chapters.text: Portuguese ships began taking captives from West Africa in the 1440s, and Portugal went on to carry more Africans across the Atlantic than any other country, mostly to Brazil. In the 1500s about one in ten people in Lisbon was Black.
chapters.image: Blue facades of waterfront buildings at Ribeira das Naus in Lisbon, Portugal, 20250604 2033 9639.jpg

chapters.heading: The Dutch West India Company
chapters.text: The Dutch West India Company, founded in 1621, traded in slaves from forts on the Gold Coast to colonies such as Suriname. The Netherlands abolished slavery in 1863, among the last in Western Europe. In 1934 the Surinamese writer Anton de Kom published a history of the colony told from the side of the enslaved.

chapters.heading: Denmark's islands
chapters.text: Denmark held colonies in the Caribbean, now the US Virgin Islands, and shipped sugar and rum home to warehouses like this one on the harbour. It was the first country to pass a law banning the trade, in 1792, though it took effect only in 1803.

chapters.heading: The capital of the trade
chapters.text: London's Royal African Company held a monopoly on the English slave trade from the 1670s, and the City financed and insured it. Black Londoners, free and enslaved, lived in the city throughout. The British Museum holds an Akan drum carried to Virginia in the 1700s.

chapters.heading: The biggest slaving port
chapters.text: By the end of the 1700s, Liverpool ships carried most of Britain's trade in enslaved people. The money is in the street names, the Town Hall and the old Exchange. Since 2007, the International Slavery Museum has stood on the dock where slaving ships were fitted out.

chapters.heading: Tobacco and sugar
chapters.text: Glasgow's “tobacco lords” grew rich on plantations in Virginia and the Caribbean worked by enslaved people. Their mansions and warehouses are the Merchant City, and streets there are still called Virginia Street and Jamaica Street.

title: Leonardo da Vinci
intro: Leonardo finished very few paintings, and they are now spread across five cities. He spent his life moving between patrons in Florence, Milan, Rome and France, often leaving work half done when something more interesting came along.
This thread follows his working life and the paintings it left behind.

chapters.heading: Apprentice
chapters.text: Leonardo trained in the workshop of Andrea del Verrocchio, a sculptor and painter who supplied Florence's churches and guild halls. Vasari tells the story that after the young Leonardo painted an angel in Verrocchio's Baptism of Christ, his master gave up painting.

chapters.heading: The Last Supper
chapters.text: He wrote to the Duke of Milan offering himself mainly as a military engineer, mentioning painting near the end. In Milan he painted the Last Supper on the refectory wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie, in an experimental technique that started flaking within his lifetime. He also turned a hall of the Sforza castle into a forest of painted trees.

chapters.heading: Lady with an Ermine
chapters.text: In Milan he also painted Cecilia Gallerani, the duke's teenage mistress, holding an ermine. It was bought for a Polish princess around 1800, the Nazis took it, and it came back to Kraków after the war. It is one of only four portraits of women by Leonardo.

chapters.heading: The battle with Michelangelo
chapters.text: Back in Florence, the republic hired Leonardo and the young Michelangelo to paint rival battle scenes on facing walls of the great council hall. Neither finished. Leonardo's experimental paint ran, and Michelangelo was called away to Rome.

chapters.heading: A drawing the size of a painting
chapters.text: The Burlington House Cartoon, a full-size chalk drawing of the Virgin, Saint Anne and the infants, was never turned into a painting. The National Gallery bought it in 1962 after a public appeal.

chapters.heading: The Mona Lisa
chapters.text: He started the portrait of Lisa del Giocondo in Florence and kept working on it for years, taking it with him to France, where he died in 1519. It became the world's most famous painting partly because it was stolen from the Louvre in 1911 and missing for two years.

image: The Last Supper Leonardo Da Vinci - High Resolution.jpg

title: Spies
intro: For a century, Europe's cities were where spies met, traded and sometimes died. Neutral capitals, divided cities and grand hotels were the places to be.
The stops run in date order, from the First World War to a poisoned cup of tea in London.

chapters.heading: A nurse before a firing squad
chapters.text: Edith Cavell, a British nurse running a clinic in occupied Brussels, helped hundreds of Allied soldiers escape to the neutral Netherlands. The Germans shot her in October 1915, and Britain made her a martyr. Historians have since found she was also passing on intelligence.

chapters.heading: Orwell's war
chapters.text: George Orwell came to Barcelona to fight against Franco. His wife Eileen worked in the office of the party militia he joined, and both were watched by Soviet-backed agents. In 1937 the militia was suppressed, and they escaped Spain just in time.
chapters.image: 13 Edifici Telefònica, av. Portal de l'Àngel - pl. Catalunya (Barcelona).jpg

chapters.heading: The neutral port
chapters.text: Portugal stayed neutral in the Second World War, and Lisbon became the last open door out of Europe. Refugees waited for ships to America, and British and German agents worked the same hotels and cafés.

chapters.heading: The Third Man
chapters.text: Postwar Vienna was split between four occupying powers, with a black market in everything. Graham Greene and Carol Reed made The Third Man there in the ruins, with the chase through the sewers and the meeting on the Prater wheel.

chapters.heading: The front line
chapters.text: Berlin was the Cold War's listening post. The Americans and British built a station on Teufelsberg, a hill made of wartime rubble, to listen into the East. On the Glienicke Bridge the two sides exchanged captured spies, starting in 1962. After 1989, East Germans could read the files the Stasi had kept on them.

chapters.heading: Radio across the Curtain
chapters.text: Radio Free Europe broadcast news into the Eastern bloc from a building beside the English Garden. Communist services planted agents on its staff, and in 1981 its offices were bombed.

chapters.heading: Between the blocs
chapters.text: Tito's Yugoslavia broke with Stalin in 1948 and belonged to neither side, which made Belgrade a place where both sides met. The café of the Hotel Moskva was a favourite.
chapters.image: Hotel Moskva and the fountain in Belgrade.jpg

chapters.heading: Reading your own file
chapters.text: Romania's Securitate had one of the largest informer networks in the bloc. The American anthropologist Katherine Verdery did fieldwork there and later read the files it kept on her, in which she appears as a spy.

chapters.heading: Polonium in Mayfair
chapters.text: Alexander Litvinenko, a former Russian security officer living in London, was poisoned with polonium in November 2006 and died three weeks later. A British inquiry concluded that the Russian state was probably behind it.

title: The Habsburgs
intro: For four hundred years one family married and inherited its way into ruling much of Europe, from Spain and the Netherlands to Bohemia and Hungary. Its palaces, crypts and art collections are still among the main sights in half a dozen cities.
The thread follows the family west to east and through to its end in 1918.

chapters.heading: Charles V
chapters.text: Charles V was born in Ghent and came of age in Brussels, ruling the Netherlands, Spain, its American colonies and the Holy Roman Empire. In 1555, worn out, he gave up his thrones in the great hall of the Coudenberg Palace in Brussels. Its remains are under the Place Royale.
chapters.image: Brussels, straatzicht Place Royale met église Saint-Jacques-sur-Coudenberg oeg2043-01020 en standbeeld van Godefroid de Bouillon foto3 2015-06-07 13.53.jpg

chapters.heading: The Spanish branch
chapters.text: Charles's son Philip II made Madrid the capital of Spain. The Spanish Habsburgs collected the paintings that became the Prado. In Las Meninas, Velázquez painted the court of Philip IV around the king's young daughter. The line ended in 1700 with Charles II, who had no children.

chapters.heading: Rudolf's court
chapters.text: Emperor Rudolf II moved his court to Prague and filled the castle with astronomers, alchemists and art. Tycho Brahe worked for him. In 1618 Protestant nobles threw two imperial governors and their secretary out of a castle window, and the Thirty Years' War began.

chapters.heading: The imperial capital
chapters.text: After the Ottoman siege of 1683, Vienna grew into the imperial capital: the Hofburg in town, Schönbrunn as the summer palace, and the Kunsthistorisches Museum for the collections. Franz Joseph reigned for 68 years, from 1848 to 1916, and his wife Elisabeth, Sisi, became a legend.
chapters.image: Hofburg Neue Burg section, Heldenplatz. Statue of Archduke Charles.jpg

chapters.heading: Austria-Hungary
chapters.text: After losing a war to Prussia, Franz Joseph agreed in 1867 to share power with Hungary: two countries under one monarch. Budapest boomed, building its parliament, opera and boulevards to rival Vienna.

chapters.heading: The end
chapters.text: Franz Joseph's only son, Rudolf, died with his young lover at Mayerling in 1889. His nephew and heir, Franz Ferdinand, was shot in Sarajevo in 1914, and the war that followed ended the empire in 1918. The family is buried in the Capuchin Crypt in Vienna.

title: Vikings
intro: For about three centuries, Scandinavians raided, traded and settled from Ireland to the Black Sea. Several of today's capitals began as their towns or were shaped by them.
The stops follow them from their homelands westward.

chapters.heading: At home
chapters.text: Most Vikings were farmers, and raiding was a summer occupation. Denmark's National Museum holds much of what survives of daily life, from weapons to jewellery.

chapters.heading: East to Byzantium
chapters.text: Swedish Vikings mostly went east, along the rivers of Russia to Constantinople and Baghdad. Silver coins from the Islamic world turn up in Swedish graves by the tens of thousands.

chapters.place: Museum of the Viking Age, Oslo
chapters.heading: The Oseberg ship
chapters.text: In 834, two women were buried in a ship at Oseberg, south of Oslo, with sledges, a cart and animals. The ship survived in the clay for eleven centuries and is now in Oslo's Viking museum, which is being rebuilt around it.

chapters.heading: Dyflin
chapters.text: Vikings set up a fortified camp on the Liffey in 841, and it grew into a trading town. In the 1970s Dublin built its civic offices on top of the excavated Viking town at Wood Quay, despite large protests.

chapters.heading: Iceland
chapters.text: Norse settlers reached Iceland around 870. The sagas say the first, Ingólfur Arnarson, threw his high-seat pillars overboard and settled where they washed up: Reykjavík. A longhouse from the period is under a hotel on Aðalstræti.

title: Plague cities
intro: The Black Death killed about a third of Europe's people in the 1340s, and plague kept coming back for nearly four hundred years. Cities invented quarantine, built churches to give thanks for surviving, and left monuments that are still there.
The stops run in date order.

chapters.heading: The Decameron
chapters.text: Plague reached Florence in 1348 and killed perhaps half the city. Boccaccio's Decameron opens with seven young women meeting three young men at Santa Maria Novella and leaving town to tell each other stories while it passes.

chapters.heading: Quarantine
chapters.text: Venice set up the first permanent plague hospital on an island in 1423 and kept ships and goods waiting forty days, quaranta giorni. After the plague of 1630–31 it built Santa Maria della Salute to give thanks.
chapters.image: (Venice) - Santa Maria della Salute - Le due cupole e i due campanili.jpg

chapters.heading: The Betrothed
chapters.text: The plague of 1630 killed about half of Milan. Alessandro Manzoni set the climax of The Betrothed, Italy's best-known novel, in the city's lazzaretto, with crowds blaming “anointers” for spreading it.
chapters.image: Dal Re, Marc'Antonio (1697-1766) - Vedute di Milano - Il lazzaretto.jpg

chapters.heading: The Great Plague
chapters.text: London's last great plague killed about a fifth of the city in 1665. Samuel Pepys recorded it in his diary, and then the Great Fire of 1666.
chapters.image: Monument to the Great Fire of London EC3R 8AH.jpg

chapters.heading: The skulls of Fontanelle
chapters.text: The plague of 1656 killed about half of Naples. Many of the dead ended up in a quarry in the Sanità district, later a cemetery. Neapolitans adopted the skulls there and cared for them in return for favours.

chapters.heading: The last great outbreak
chapters.text: In 1720 a ship carrying plague was let into Marseille's port, reportedly because the merchants who owned its cargo pushed to skip quarantine. Around half the city died. It was the last major plague outbreak in Western Europe.

image: The Triumph of Death by Pieter Bruegel the Elder.jpg

title: World's fairs
intro: For a century, cities staged world's fairs to show off: new technology, new architecture, and themselves. Many of the buildings were meant to be temporary, and some of the best known are still standing.
The stops run in date order.

chapters.heading: Barcelona's first fair
chapters.text: Barcelona held a universal exhibition in 1888 on the site of a hated military citadel, which became Ciutadella Park. Eduardo Mendoza's novel City of Marvels is set in the city that grew around it.

chapters.heading: Paris three times
chapters.text: Paris built the Eiffel Tower as the entrance to the 1889 fair, and it was meant to come down after twenty years. The 1900 fair brought the first Métro line. At the 1937 fair the Soviet and German pavilions faced each other, and Picasso's Guernica hung in the Spanish one.
chapters.image: Eiffel tower at Exposition Universelle, Paris, 1889.jpg

chapters.heading: The Ibero-American Exposition
chapters.text: Seville's 1929 fair was for Spain and its former American colonies. Its centrepiece, the semicircular Plaza de España with a tiled bench for every province, is now one of the city's best-known sights.

chapters.heading: Mies's pavilion
chapters.text: For the 1929 fair on Montjuïc, Mies van der Rohe built the German pavilion: marble, glass, steel and almost nothing else. It was taken down after the fair and rebuilt on the same site in 1986.

chapters.heading: The Empire Exhibition
chapters.text: Glasgow's 1938 Empire Exhibition filled Bellahouston Park with modernist pavilions and a 90-metre tower. Twelve million people came. Little of it was kept.
chapters.image: 1938 Empire Exhibition view west along Scottish Avenue.jpg

chapters.heading: The fair that never opened
chapters.text: Mussolini planned a world's fair for 1942 to mark twenty years of Fascism, and began a new district south of Rome for it. The war stopped it, and the district, EUR, was finished after the war.
chapters.image: Palazzo della civiltà del lavoro (EUR, Rome) (5904657870).jpg

chapters.heading: The Atomium
chapters.text: Brussels' 1958 fair, the first after the war, was about the peaceful atom. Its symbol, a 102-metre model of an iron crystal, was supposed to be dismantled afterwards and is still there.

chapters.heading: Feeding the planet
chapters.text: Milan's Expo 2015 was about food. The site, outside the city at Rho, is being turned into a science and research district.

title: Olympic cities
intro: The modern Olympics began in Athens in 1896, and European cities have used them since to rebuild, to show off, and once to make propaganda. Most of the stadiums are still in use.
The stops run in date order.

chapters.heading: The first modern Games
chapters.text: Pierre de Coubertin's revived Olympics opened in 1896 in Athens' ancient stadium, rebuilt in white marble. The Greek water carrier Spyridon Louis won the first marathon.

chapters.heading: Hitler's Games
chapters.text: The Nazis used the 1936 Games to show the world a confident Germany. Jesse Owens, a Black American, won four gold medals in their new stadium.

chapters.heading: The skater from Oslo
chapters.text: Sonja Henie from Oslo won figure-skating gold at three Winter Olympics in a row, from 1928 to 1936, then became a Hollywood star. Oslo hosted the Winter Games in 1952.
chapters.image: Holmenkollbakken - no-nb digifoto 20150625 00168 NB MIT FNR 11656 B.jpg

chapters.heading: Helsinki 1952
chapters.text: Helsinki finally hosted the Games in 1952, after the 1940 Olympics were cancelled by the war. The Soviet Union competed for the first time, and the Czech runner Emil Zátopek won the 5,000 metres, the 10,000 metres and the marathon in eight days.

chapters.heading: The cheerful Games
chapters.text: West Germany wanted 1972 to be the opposite of 1936: pastel colours, Otl Aicher's pictograms, a tent-like stadium roof. On 5 September, Palestinian gunmen took Israeli athletes hostage in the Olympic village, and eleven of them were killed.

chapters.heading: The city rebuilt
chapters.text: Barcelona used the 1992 Games to open itself to the sea, replacing old industrial waterfront with beaches and a new Olympic village. It is still the model other host cities point to.
chapters.image: Aerial view of Somorrostro Beach and Port Olympic in Barcelona, Spain (51227006624).jpg

chapters.heading: East London
chapters.text: London put its 2012 Games in Stratford, in the East End, on old industrial land. Zaha Hadid's aquatics centre is now a public pool.

title: Punk
intro: Punk started in London in 1976 and spread across Europe within a couple of years: three chords, cheap clubs, home-made records. In most cities it was also about something local, from boredom to the Troubles.
The stops run roughly in the order punk arrived.

chapters.heading: Year zero
chapters.text: Malcolm McLaren and Vivienne Westwood's shop at 430 King's Road dressed the Sex Pistols. The scene played the 100 Club and the Roxy, and by 1977 the Clash were singing about London itself.

chapters.heading: Forty people
chapters.text: In June 1976 the Sex Pistols played the Lesser Free Trade Hall to a small crowd. Members of Buzzcocks, Joy Division and the Fall were there, or said they were, and Manchester's bands came out of it.

chapters.heading: Good Vibrations
chapters.text: In Belfast during the Troubles, punk was one of the few scenes Catholic and Protestant kids shared. Terri Hooley's Good Vibrations record shop put out records by local bands, including the Undertones' “Teenage Kicks”.

chapters.heading: Ça plane pour moi
chapters.text: Plastic Bertrand's “Ça plane pour moi” was a Europe-wide hit in 1977, a novelty punk single fronted by a Belgian drummer.

chapters.heading: Zurich burns
chapters.text: Zurich's punk band Kleenex, later LiLiPUT, were four women whose records came out on Rough Trade in London. In 1980 young people rioted for a cultural centre of their own, and got the Rote Fabrik.

chapters.heading: West Berlin
chapters.text: In walled-in West Berlin, Kreuzberg's SO36 club was the centre of the punk and post-punk scene. Nina Hagen had come over from the East in 1976.

chapters.heading: Ebba Grön
chapters.text: Ebba Grön came out of a youth centre in the Stockholm suburb of Rågsved. “Staten och kapitalet”, the state and capital, became a protest anthem.

chapters.heading: Rokk í Reykjavík
chapters.text: Iceland's punk scene was tiny but loud. Purrkur Pillnikk and other bands appear in the 1982 film Rokk í Reykjavík. Jón Gnarr, a teenage punk at the time, became the city's mayor in 2010.

title: The Ottoman frontier
intro: For more than three centuries the Ottoman Empire pushed into Europe and Europe pushed back. The frontier ran through cities that changed hands, held sieges and still carry the marks.
The stops run in date order, from the fall of Constantinople to Greek independence.

chapters.heading: Constantinople falls
chapters.text: Mehmed II's cannons broke the thousand-year-old land walls of Constantinople in May 1453. He made the city his capital and built the Topkapı Palace above the Bosphorus.

chapters.heading: The gate to Hungary
chapters.text: In 1456 John Hunyadi held Belgrade's fortress against Mehmed II; church bells still ring at noon in memory of the victory. In 1521 Suleiman the Magnificent took it.

chapters.heading: Vlad the Impaler
chapters.text: Vlad III of Wallachia, who fought the Ottomans with notorious cruelty, is the first ruler known to have signed a document in Bucharest. His court's ruins are in the Old Town.

chapters.heading: Ottoman Buda
chapters.text: The Ottomans held Buda for 145 years. They left Turkish baths that are still in use, and the tomb of the dervish Gül Baba, which is still a place of pilgrimage.
chapters.image: Rudas Baths central part and Gellert Hill in Tabán, 2016 Budapest.jpg

chapters.place: Arsenale and the Grand Canal, Venice
chapters.heading: Lepanto
chapters.text: Venice traded with the Ottomans and fought them. Its Arsenale built much of the Christian fleet that sank the Ottoman navy at Lepanto in 1571. Turkish merchants had their own trading house on the Grand Canal, the Fondaco dei Turchi.
chapters.image: (Venice) Battaglia di Lepanto - Andrea Vicentino - Correr Museum.jpg

chapters.heading: The second siege
chapters.text: In 1683 an Ottoman army besieged Vienna for two months. On 12 September a relief army under the Polish king Jan III Sobieski charged down from the Kahlenberg and broke it.

chapters.heading: Sobieski's palace
chapters.text: Jan III Sobieski came home a hero and built Wilanów as his summer palace, decorated with scenes of his victories.

chapters.heading: The Parthenon explodes
chapters.text: In 1687 a Venetian shell hit Ottoman gunpowder stored in the Parthenon and blew out its middle. In 1821 the Greeks rose against Ottoman rule, and Athens became the capital of an independent Greece in 1834.

image: Relief of Vienna 1683 - Wien Museum - 2 (photo by Andrew Nash).jpg

title: Byzantium
intro: The Roman Empire carried on in the east for a thousand years after Rome fell, ruled from Constantinople. The Byzantines called themselves Romans, and their capital was the richest city in Christendom.
Much of what survives was taken elsewhere. This thread starts in the city and follows the loot.

chapters.heading: Hagia Sophia
chapters.text: Justinian's Hagia Sophia, finished in 537, had the largest dome in the world for nearly a thousand years. It became a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020. Its mosaics are still visible upstairs.

chapters.heading: The walls
chapters.text: Three lines of land walls, built in the 400s, kept Constantinople safe for a thousand years. Most of their six kilometres still stand.

chapters.heading: The Fourth Crusade
chapters.text: In 1204 a crusader army meant for Egypt turned on Constantinople instead, sacked it, and put a Latin emperor on its throne. Venice, which had built the fleet, took a large share of the loot.
chapters.image: The Entry of the Crusaders into Constantinople - 1840 - Eugène Delacroix - Louvre - Inv 3821.jpg

chapters.heading: The loot in Venice
chapters.text: The four bronze horses over St Mark's came from Constantinople's Hippodrome, and the porphyry Tetrarchs set into the basilica's corner were taken from the city too. Venice built its sea empire partly on what it took.
chapters.image: Horses of Basilica San Marco bright.jpg

chapters.heading: The Barberini Ivory
chapters.text: An ivory panel of an emperor on horseback, made in Constantinople in the 500s, passed through a Roman cardinal's collection to the Louvre.

chapters.heading: The Archangel Michael
chapters.text: The largest Byzantine ivory panel to survive, an archangel holding a sceptre and orb, is in the British Museum.
